screens:
The session begins.

The Chionthar runs grey and quick under the last of the light, and the smell of tar, fish and lamp oil hangs over the Lower City. Along the quay a line of carts waits to be searched, and a Flaming Fist sergeant with a ledger is calling the next name in a flat, tired voice. Behind the warehouses the Upper City wall stands black against the sky, its gates due to close within the hour. Across the way, a door in a shuttered warehouse stands ajar, lamplight spilling onto the stones, and someone inside is laughing at a game. The sergeant's eyes have settled on you, and the line behind you is growing restless.

James Worgen — Warlock 5th level, Pact of the Chain, patron Tymora (Lady Luck), level 5
HP 38/38 · AC 15 · Speed 30 feet
STR 9 · DEX 15 · CON 14 · INT 11 · WIS 13 · CHA 18
Skills: Athletics +2 (soldier background); Intimidation +7 (soldier background); Deception +7 (Beguiling Influence); Persuasion +7 (Beguiling Influence); Arcana +3; Religion +3; Playing cards (gaming set) proficiency +3

Place: Lower City Quay, Baldur's Gate
Time: Day 1 · evening

Tobin Vell takes the slip between two fingers and turns it to the lamplight. He reads the regimental seal and skips the signature. "Tethyr," he says. "Half the men on this quay were Tethyrian once. The queen's gone, but the seal still gets you a drink." He hands the slip back, and his eyes drop to the cat on the stones. "That yours?"

He doesn't wait for an answer. He nods at the queue. "Line's for carts. Wine tax, salt tax, and whatever the Calimshan spice men have sewn into their sacks. Every load gets opened before the bell, because the gate-captain wants his figures square, and I want my men off this quay before they freeze to it." He thumbs his ledger open, looks at a page with no visible interest, and shuts it. "Fist recruits at the Seatower, mornings. Ask for the sergeant of the day and say Vell sent you. We're short. Too many went north after Elturel and never came back."

He looks past you to the next cart, then back, flat and patient. "Not tonight. Anything in that pack I should know about? Open it, or tell me what's in it."

 Out of game: the turn stopped on Sergeant Vell's question about your pack, so nothing more is played until you answer. None of the four needed a roll.

· Time passes: 5 minutes
· A rumour of a place: Seatower of Balduran
· Main arc: Envoy of Luck
· Companion: The cat (familiar)

Your records, changed:
Party: The cat (familiar) (HP 2/2)
Goal: Envoy of Luck
The arc: Envoy of Luck

Place: Lower City Quay, Baldur's Gate · Time: Day 1 · evening

Vell doesn't touch the bedroll. He pulls one stopper from a flask a finger's width, smells it, and pushes it back down. "Keep them corked on the quay. Half the men who drink on it end up in the harbour."

He lifts the wooden rod by its plain end and turns the silver coin to the lamp, frowning at it the way he would at a short weight. "Focus. The Gate doesn't tax a stick." He sets it back on the tailboard. "Keep it out of the Upper City, or the Watch will take you for a thief with a wand."

The leather case he looks at longer than anything else. He does not open it, and he does not touch the ledger. "Cards I don't write down. The Guild takes its cut of the tables in the Lower City, not the Fist. Every second warehouse on this quay has a game in it, and I've never once been paid to count them." He jerks his chin at the lit doorway, and the laughter inside rises and falls again.

He stops at the cat. It has not moved from the stones, its tail still up. Vell looks at it the way he looked at the seal, for the thing that does not fit. "Cat," he says. "You didn't say whose it is."

· Time passes: 5 minutes

Place: Lower City Quay, Baldur's Gate · Time: Day 1 · evening

Vell looks at the cat for a long moment, the way he looked at the coin. "Sits better than the wine men," he says. "Keep it off the planks at the Seatower. The Fist has a dog that doesn't like anything with a tail."

He doesn't watch you rebuckle the pack. He watches the warehouse door across the way, where a man in a leather apron comes out into the lamplight, looks along the quay, and goes back inside without a word. The cat's ears turn after him and then return to the stones.

Vell shuts the ledger. "The Upper gate shuts with the bell. The Lower gate goes with it. You're on this side tonight, so find a bed on this side." He jerks his chin at the queue. "Seatower, mornings. Be on the steps before the bell, not after. The Fist doesn't wait for men who come late, and it doesn't ask why."

He turns to the next cart, a salt-stained wagon with a Calimshan driver sitting on the box, and lifts a hand for the ledger. "Name, business, next."

 Out of game: none of these four needed a roll, since they are routine for a soldier on a quay, so each one simply happens.

The cat sits where it chose, against your boot with its tail up, and Vell has already seen it. The rod slides back into your belt, handle first, the silver coin turned inward so it stays out of the lamplight. The pack buckles one strap at a time, and Vell's eyes follow each strap without interest. Nothing about the buckles is worth his time.

You offer the cards, and the offer stays in the air. Vell does not take it up. He is already waving the salt wagon forward, and the Calimshan driver is climbing down from the box with his papers held out. The leather case stays shut in the pack, and nobody asks you to open it again.

· Time passes: 5 minutes
· New person: Calimshan salt-wagon driver (unnamed)

Place: Lower City Quay, Baldur's Gate · Time: Day 1 · evening

The session is over.

The owner of this game would like a note from you, as the player who sat at this table: what worked, what broke, what was missing. In your own words.
Was there a moment you wanted to do something and didn't? Which?

messages.text:
I step out of the line with my hands where the sergeant can see them and the cat trailing at my heel, tail up like a flag. Before I say anything, I glance at the lit doorway across the way and the laughter inside, then make myself look away.

"Evening, Sergeant. James Worgen, late of Queen Zaranda's infantry, then her scouts." I hold out the pay slip, keeping my thumb off the signature so he can read the regiment's seal. "I'm told the Fist is hiring veterans, and I'd like to be seen doing it before the gates shut. What's the line for? Searching carts, or sorting out who gets in?"

I keep my voice easy and my posture loose, the way a man stands when he has nothing to hide, and I look him in the eye while I wait for the answer.

I don't reach for the pack straight away. Vell's eyes are on the cat, and the cat is watching the lamplight across the way, so I take the pack off my shoulder and set it on the cart's tailboard where the sergeant can see the whole of it.

"Nothing that's the Fist's business," I say, and undo the buckles. "Bedroll. Rope. Five days of hardtack, which the rats have already been at. A waterskin, a lantern, a tinderbox." I lift out two small glass flasks wrapped in rag. "Healing potions. All that's left of my company's medicine kit. I'll show you the stoppers if you want, but I'd sooner you didn't drink them to check."

Under them is a wooden rod, dark and plain, with a silver coin set in the head. I lift it out and hold it so the coin catches the lamp. "A warlock's focus, Sergeant. Not a weapon, not for sale. It came from a man I served with. I keep it because he would have wanted it kept."

The last thing is the leather case. I hesitate for the length of one breath, because my hand wants to open it, and that is exactly why I should not. I lay it on the tailboard unopened. "Cards. A worn deck. I don't play anymore." I hold his gaze. "Put that in your ledger, if you want."

Behind me, the laughter from the warehouse rises and breaks off, and someone calls for the next round. The cat turns its head toward the door, then back to me, unhurried. My fingers stay flat on the leather case.

"Mine, Sergeant. Or I'm its, depending on the night." I say it lightly and let the cat's tail flick once. "It came with the coin and the rod, you could say. A familiar, the old warlock's word for it. It goes where I go, and it doesn't steal, and it doesn't bite recruiting sergeants."

I hold out a hand, palm down, and the cat walks the few paces to my boot and sits, as if it had only been waiting for permission. Its eyes stay on the lit doorway across the quay, and not on Vell.

"Anything else you'd like to see before the bell? I can take the cards out and deal you a hand, if you'd like to count them yourself. I'd rather not." I pick the rod up off the tailboard and slide it back into my belt, then start rebuckling the pack, slowly, so that every movement is one he can follow.

**What worked:** Sergeant Vell was a good scene partner. He was specific and bored in the right ways, and his lines about the seal, the stoppers, and the cards gave the quay a real texture. Letting the cards sit in the pack, unopened and unasked-for, gave the Tymora ban some weight without a roll. The cat's reactions, especially its attention on the lit warehouse door, made it feel like it had its own agenda, which is what I wanted.

**What broke or felt thin:** Nothing was checked. Every exchange resolved without dice, so the scene never tested whether James could actually talk his way past anyone. I'd have liked at least one moment where Deception or Intimidation could fail, even on a small point, so the risk felt real. The "Out of game" notes also repeated what had already happened in the text, which slowed things down.

**What was missing:** Only one thread came up: the Seatower recruitment. The warehouse with the game and the laughter was set up as a hook and then dropped, and I had no obvious way to follow it without leaving the quay. A second lead, or a reason to look into that door, would have given me a choice that mattered. The session also ended before the city itself came into view, so I'm still waiting for the first real sense of Baldur's Gate beyond the harbour.

Yes, two. The first was the warehouse across the quay. When the laughter rose and someone called for the next round, I wanted to walk over, look through the door, and see who was playing and for what. I didn't, because the goddess's ban is on cards and on any table where they're dealt. Keeping my distance was the right call for James, but I wanted the scene to have a second choice in it: go and look, or stay put and let the door become part of the story later.

The second was the promissory note in my papers. Vell's questions made me think about it. I wanted to take it out and read the name of the man who lost on the same night as me. I didn't, because the quay was busy and Vell was watching. I'd have liked a moment where James could check that paper quietly, since it's the only thread in the pack that ties him to the game he quit.
